correctness.rationale: The full-translation Fourier multiplier is computed by Plancherel and finite character orthogonality. Inverse DFT makes constancy off zero frequency equivalent to equal nonzero-lag coefficients; the paired equations give all three exhaustive phase-weight cases and positivity. Requiring constancy at zero gives full-space case. Zero-one antipodal transversals, subgroup parity, and exact erasure extrema follow by elementary group and cosine ordering; finite checks and independent matrix corroboration are packaged.

originality.rationale: The three inspected 2017 open full texts cover subgroup frame conditions, normalization procedures, and Fourier-indicator wavelet tiling. They do not state the combined arbitrary-weight two-tap phase classification and scale-packet erasure. Closest published research hits concern STFT support, spectrogram Jacobians, and two-character Fourier-frame erasures, which do not logically imply the claimed affine system theorem. Historical priority remains provisional, notably under filter-bank terminology and the partially accessible 2017 subgroup source.
residual_risks: The earliest complete finite wavelet subgroup paper by Ghaani Farashahi (2017) was accessible only as abstract/bibliography, so a hidden exactly equivalent two-tap theorem cannot be excluded; its stated scope is subgroup-generated frames.
A finite filter-bank, Calderón-sum, or short-filter treatment could express the equivalent arbitrary-weight condition under a different name.
No independent literature-priority or expert audit has been performed.

value.rationale: A two-tap difference generator is the minimal local zero-mean wavelet. The theorem completely characterizes exactly tight choices among all nonnegative dilation weights and complex phases, gives a sharp minimal-scale construction and exact count, arithmetic subgroup eligibility, and design-independent sharp scale-packet erasure stability. These solve a natural finite-wavelet design problem with meaningful full/mean-zero distinction, beyond computing a single isolated sample.
